name: World Spine Care (HLI, 2026)
summary: Runs clinics giving free physiotherapy and chiropractic care for back and neck pain in low- and middle-income countries. The Happier Lives Institute's back-of-the-envelope estimate (WELLBYs per $1,000), rebuilt from the figures in its report.

source.title: Investigating three ways to reduce the global pain burden (pain cause exploration 3)
source.license: © Happier Lives Institute; no licence published. Numbers cited as facts with their source.

resources.title: HLI, Investigating three ways to reduce the global pain burden (2026), section 3
resources.note: HLI publishes no public spreadsheet for this estimate: the model is built from the inputs and figures stated in the report's text, each quoted on its row. HLI's figure is for a donation restricted to World Spine Care's clinics in low- and middle-income countries (Botswana, the Dominican Republic and others), not its work in Canada.

sections.title: Effect per patient treated for a year
Staff pay below market
sections.explainer: charityevals' step, not the evaluator's: with credit by share of resources on, staff's pay below what they could earn elsewhere counts as an in-kind contribution and gets its share of the outcome. Off by default.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained when musculoskeletal pain is treated (0–10 scale)

source.title: HLI report
source.quote: We base our estimate on the 1.17 life satisfaction effect reported by Boonstra et al. (2013)

rows.explainer: Boonstra et al. (2013) found people with chronic musculoskeletal pain 0.7 points less satisfied with life on a 1–7 scale than the general public, 1.17 on a 0–10 scale. HLI notes part of the gap is likely age, education and employment, and calls the resulting estimate generous: it assumes treatment removes the whole gap for a year.

rows.label: Household spillover, as a share of the patient's own effect
rows.explainer: HLI uses its psychotherapy spillover, having none for pain treatment ("16.24% spillover for an average non-recipient household size of 3.33 people in LMICs").

source.title: HLI report
source.quote: 16.24% spillover for an average non-recipient household size of 3.33 people in LMICs

source.title: HLI report
source.quote: apply our standard 0.51 (49% discount) replication adjustment

rows.label: WELLBYs per patient treated for a year
rows.explainer: HLI: "This gives an estimated 0.92 total adjusted WELLBYs per person treated".

rows.label: Cost to treat a patient for a year

source.title: HLI report
source.quote: Our best guess was that it costs between $44 and $63 to treat a patient for one year

rows.explainer: From World Spine Care's clinic data for Botswana and the Dominican Republic ($13–17 a visit). HLI's generous estimate assumes only three visits per patient; more visits would raise the cost. HLI gives the range; the middle, $53.50, is ours.

rows.label: WELLBYs per $1,000
rows.explainer: HLI: "an overall cost-effectiveness of 15–21 WELLBYs per $1,000 donated", the two ends of its cost range; the central figure at the middle cost is ours. The benefit comes within the year of treatment, so there is nothing to discount.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of program cost
rows.explainer: Clinics run mostly on clinicians' time: our judgment of the staff share of cost.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: Most clinicians are volunteers from high-income countries on below-market stipends (HLI, section 3), so the gap to their usual pay is large. Our judgment.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff per dollar of cost (in-kind donation)
Share of the full cost paid in cash
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, staff's forgone pay counts as part of the cost, and staff get their share of the outcome. Off, this is 100%.

rows.label: WELLBYs per dollar
rows.explainer: The figure per dollar above; with credit by share of resources, times the share of the full cost paid in cash (staff's forgone pay is the rest).
